title: Stealing minds
hook: deceiving someone, even without taking money

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was honest weights: one standard, in the bag and at home. How did your one deal go? Today, a theft where no money changes hands at all. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

A friend is passing your door. You call out: come in, stay for dinner! You say it warmly. You also know, for certain, that he can't; he's on his way somewhere and will say no. He leaves feeling cared for. You leave looking generous. Nothing was taken from him. No coin, no object, nothing anyone could report. And yet the Talmud uses this exact scene as an example of stealing. What could have been stolen? Today's word is the name the rabbis gave to it.
screen: `COME IN, STAY FOR DINNER!` → `YOU KNOW HE CAN'T.` → `WHAT WAS STOLEN?`

segments.voice: Genevat da'at. Literally, the stealing of knowledge, or of the mind. It means creating a false impression in someone, getting credit or goodwill you didn't earn. Turn it four ways. First, the rule. In tractate Chullin, the sage Shmuel says it is forbidden to steal the mind of any person, and he adds that this includes a person who isn't Jewish. The rule isn't about one's own community. It's about every mind. Second, the examples. The Talmud gives small, domestic ones. Don't press a friend to eat with you when you know he won't. Don't load him with gifts you know he'll refuse. Don't open a barrel of wine and let him think it's in his honor, when you were opening it to sell anyway. Every example is a kindness that isn't real. Third, an old story. In the Second Book of Samuel, David's son Absalom stands by the city gate. Whoever comes with a case, he greets, kisses, and tells: if only I were judge, you'd get justice. The verse sums it up: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." He took nothing from their purses. He took their trust, and used it to turn them against his father. Fourth, why it's theft. Money stolen can be paid back. A false picture planted in someone's head keeps working after you've gone: they decide, trust, vote, buy, based on what you let them believe. The tradition treats a person's understanding as something that belongs to them. Mislead it, and you've reached in and taken something.
screen: `STEALING THE MIND.` · `ANY PERSON'S MIND.` · `A KINDNESS THAT ISN'T REAL.` · `ABSALOM STOLE THEIR HEARTS.` · then, large: `DON'T STEAL MINDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't mislead anyone today. Before the day fills up, look ahead at it. Sit, and breathe. Let the day's conversations come to mind one by one: the email, the meeting, the sale, the dinner, the photo you might post. Ask of each one: is there a place where I'm tempted to let someone believe something that isn't so? An offer I don't mean, a busy-ness I'm exaggerating, a compliment I'll give to get something back. Find one. Decide now what the plain version sounds like. The bell holds the time.
Genevat da'at. The stealing of the mind: deceiving someone, even when no money is taken. Today's word.
Your line: don't steal minds. Today, when you find that one place, say the plain version, even if it makes you look a little less generous. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish law codes treat genevat da'at as a prohibition in its own right, and it's discussed in contexts from shopkeeping and advertising to everyday social courtesies.

original.note: Hebrew: stealing of the mind, of knowledge.

trapdoor: what you thought: stealing means taking someone's things.
what it means: genevat da'at: planting a false impression, taking goodwill or trust you didn't earn.
what a scholar hears: Chullin 94a, in Shmuel's name, with its examples of the invitation and the barrel; and Absalom, who stole the hearts of Israel.
